exercise.name: 4 Cone Single Foot Lateral Hops
aliases: Lateral hurdle hop and stick (single leg)

reference.title: 4 Cone Single Foot Lateral Hops (male)
reference.listing: Video (35 s); data sheet: body part Plyometrics, equipment Body weight (plus 4 small cones), exercise type Aerobic
reference.note: Reference used only to identify the movement. No GymVisual media is stored here; this rig, model and animation are original.

exercise.laterality: Unilateral (one leg hops down the line and back, then switch legs)

muscleNotes.calves_r: Soleus and gastrocnemius drive each push-off from the ball of the foot and control the heel on landing; soleus activity rose with faster lateral hopping (Suwanmana 2026). The calf region here also stands in for tibialis anterior and the peroneals, which steady the ankle against rolling (not separate rig regions).
muscleNotes.quads_r: Absorb each landing as the knee bends from about 30 degrees at contact to about 60 degrees (Markström 2020), then extend for the next push-off.
muscleNotes.glute_max_r: Active before and during lateral hop landings (Webster 2016); extends the hip on push-off.
muscleNotes.hamstrings_r: Help control hip and knee flexion on landing (inferred, not measured for this drill).
muscleNotes.adductors_r: Help push the body toward the far side when hopping back toward the free leg (inferred).
muscleNotes.glute_med_r: Keeps the pelvis level and the knee over the midfoot on single-leg landings (Neamatallah 2018 links it to hip adduction control).
muscleNotes.core: Brace the trunk so the chest stays over the foot.
muscleNotes.obliques_r: Limit side lean of the trunk on landing.
muscleNotes.obliques_l: Limit side lean of the trunk on landing.
muscleNotes.hamstrings_l: Hold the free knee bent with the foot lifted behind.
muscleNotes.hip_flexors_l: Keep the free thigh from dropping so the foot stays off the floor.

breathing.pattern: Breathe naturally and rhythmically. Breathe out lightly on each take-off or landing and take a quick breath during each stick. Brace the trunk but do not hold the breath for the whole line.
breathing.cadence: One hop about every 1.4 s in the animation (about 0.3 s in the air, then a short stick)

prescription.reps: One pass down the four cones and back per set (8 hops)
prescription.endRangeHold: Stick each landing for a beat (about 1 s in practice; shorter in the animation) before the next hop
prescription.staticOption: Single-leg balance or hops over a floor line or flat markers
prescription.frequency: 2 sessions per week, 48-72 h between hard lower-body plyometric sessions
prescription.tempo: Hop, land soft, stick, then hop again; never rush a hop off a wobbly landing
prescription.volume: Count foot contacts: about 80-100 per session for beginners, up to 120-140 for advanced athletes

cues.text: Stand tall on one leg beside the first cone, knee soft and hips level. The other knee is bent with the foot lifted behind you.
Push off from the ball of the foot and hop sideways just high and wide enough to clear the cone.
Land quietly on the ball of the foot, then let the heel settle as the knee and hip bend.
Keep the knee over the middle of the foot: no caving inward.
Stick the landing for a beat, hips level and chest up, then change direction.
Hop back the other way down the line, still on the same foot.
Eyes forward, not down at the cones. Use the arms lightly for balance.
Soft landing every time: about a third of a bend at contact, then sink to about 60 degrees.
Last hop: stick it, hips level, free foot still off the floor.
Stand tall, reset, then repeat or switch to the left leg.

mistakes.mistake: Knee caves inward on landing (dynamic valgus)
mistakes.fix: Shrink the hop or the cone spacing. Think knee over the second toe and push the knee slightly out.

mistakes.mistake: Stiff, loud landing with a nearly straight knee
mistakes.fix: Land on the forefoot with the knee already bent about 30 degrees, then sink into the landing.

mistakes.mistake: Hip drops or the trunk leans far over the landing leg
mistakes.fix: Keep the pelvis level and the chest over the foot. Lower the cones until you can.

mistakes.mistake: Extra stutter hop or the free foot touching down
mistakes.fix: Slow down and earn a full stick before the next hop.

mistakes.mistake: Rolling onto the outside of the foot
mistakes.fix: Land on the ball of the foot with the foot pointing forward. Narrow the spacing and stop if the ankle feels unstable.

mistakes.mistake: Clipping cones by hopping too low or watching the feet
mistakes.fix: Look ahead, lift the knee and drive from the ankle. Start with flat markers.

mistakes.mistake: Racing through reps as form fades
mistakes.fix: Stop the set when technique declines.

kinematics.norm: About 30-37° in side hop landings (controls 30°, ACL-reconstructed knees 37°)

kinematics.peak: ≈60° at the bottom of each landing
kinematics.norm: Peak knee flexion about 59-63° in side hop landings

kinematics.peak: Knee over the midfoot (frontal-plane knee angle not modelled; the rig knee is a hinge)
kinematics.norm: No medial collapse; peak knee abduction only about 3° in side hop landings

kinematics.peak: ≈57° at the bottom of the landing (trunk ≈18° from vertical)
kinematics.norm: Soft hip bend with the chest over the foot; ACL-reconstructed limbs used more hip and trunk flexion

kinematics.setup: Knee ≈88°, foot ≈31 cm off the floor, behind the support leg
kinematics.norm: Knee bent, foot lifted behind or beside the support leg
Side hop test lines 30-40 cm apart; small cones about 15 cm tall (spacing and height are not stated for this drill)
Four hops of one cone spacing each, then back to the start

kinematics.peak: ≈0.5 s held after the landing (≈0.9 s at the turn); ≈1.1 s on the ground per hop
kinematics.norm: 1-2 s stick in coaching videos; 2-3 s in clinical hop-for-distance testing; no study sets a stick time for this drill
Just high enough to clear the cone

cautions: Demanding for an unstable ankle: side hop performance separates people with chronic ankle instability, so start with floor lines and narrow spacing and stop if the ankle gives way.
Stop with pain, swelling or a joint that feels unstable.
Use a firm, non-slip floor and soft, collapsible cones so a clipped cone cannot trip you.
modify: After ACL reconstruction or other knee surgery: only once cleared for hopping, usually in late rehab.
Not with an acute sprain or strain, joint effusion, an unhealed ligament, cartilage or bone injury, or too little base strength.
Beginners, older adults, heavier individuals and anyone with poor single-leg balance: start with two-leg hops or balance work.
regressions: Two-leg lateral hops over the cones.
Single-leg hops over a floor line or flat markers.
Single-leg balance for 30 s, then single hops with a long stick.
progressions: Faster hops once every landing stays quiet and the knee stays over the foot.
